svg.text: A2A: The Agent2Agent Protocol
A2A Architecture — discovery, communication, and the agent life cycle
Essence: A2A is a shared language that lets any agent — built with any framework —
wrap itself as an A2A agent and work with any other A2A agent over standard web tech.
🌐 A common language for agents
A2A hides the messy details of agent workflows behind one shared language: standardized
data structures and methods for talking to the outside world.
It runs on standard web technology, so independent systems can talk over:
HTTP · JSON-RPC · gRPC · Server-Sent Events (SSE)
Build an agent in any framework, then wrap it as an A2A agent — now it works
with every other A2A agent, no custom glue code needed.
🤝 The simple system: Agent A asks Agent B
We build a small system where Agent A needs Agent B to do something.
Agent A is the client agent — it makes the request and usually talks to the end user.
Agent B is the remote agent (the A2A server) — it does the actual work.
Agent A
Client agent
Agent B
Remote agent (A2A server)
sends a request
🪪 Discovery: the Agent Card
How does Agent A find Agent B and learn what it can do? Every A2A agent publishes an
Agent Card — a JSON file, usually hosted at a well-known URL:
/.well-known/agent-card.json
It is the agent's digital business card — like robots.txt for web crawlers, or a
Swagger / OpenAPI definition for REST APIs, but made for agent capabilities.
Agent B's card tells Agent A everything needed to start a conversation:
• Name and what the agent can do
• Which protocol version it uses
• The URI and protocol bindings, plus supported media types
• Special capabilities: streaming, push notifications, custom extensions
• How to authenticate
(For this course we assume we already know each agent's URL.)
🔌 How they actually talk
The card names the URI and protocol bindings to use. Agent A sends requests to
that URI over whichever binding Agent B supports. A2A allows three bindings:
JSON-RPC · gRPC · HTTP JSON (REST-like)
⚙️ Four execution modes
Agent A and Agent B can communicate in four execution modes:
Synchronous
Wait for an
immediate reply
Asynchronous
Proceed without
blocking for a reply
Streaming
Send a continuous
data flow
Push
Notifications
Alert when a
specific event occurs
① Synchronous: the Message object
To begin, Agent A sends a Message wrapped in a send-message request, using the
message/send method. A Message is one turn in the conversation — like Agent A
asking a question. It carries two things:
Role
who is speaking — user or agent
Parts
the content: text, a file, multimodal data, or JSON
If the request is simple and finishes fast, Agent B just replies with a Message.
② Asynchronous: the Task object
For a bigger or slower request, we do not want to block Agent A. Instead of a Message,
Agent B replies with a Task — the job it needs to do. A Task has an ID, a
context ID that links it back to the message, and a Status showing where the job is.
The Status moves through a life cycle:
In progress
Terminal states
submitted
working
input-required
completed
or
failed
Agent A gets the task ID, then polls task/get for updates. Note: Agent B decides
whether to return a Task or a Message — so Agent A must handle both cases.
When the Task is completed, its output sits in the artifacts field. An Artifact is like a
Message: it has an Artifact ID and Parts holding the real response content.
③ Streaming with Server-Sent Events (SSE)
Polling works, but it is not efficient when you want quick updates. If Agent B's card says
streaming: true, Agent A calls message/stream instead. The connection stays open
and Agent B pushes updates as they happen:
• Task status update events — "I am working on part X"; "the task is now completed".
• Task artifact update events — a large result streamed in chunks, paragraph by paragraph.
The user sees live progress, or the answer appears as it is being generated.
④ Push notifications (webhooks & callbacks)
What if you have no idea when — or if — Agent B will reply? Use webhook push
notifications with the task/pushNotificationConfig/set method, or add the config
when sending the first message.
Agent A gives a callback URL. Agent B actively pushes a notification to that URL when
the task state changes or an artifact is ready. The card advertises pushNotifications: true.
📡 2026 intel
Google donated A2A — the spec, SDKs, and tooling — to the Linux Foundation on
June 23, 2025. Founding members: AWS, Cisco, Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP,
and ServiceNow.
By its one-year mark in 2026, 150+ organizations back the standard, with deep
integration across Google, Microsoft, and AWS and real production deployments.
Spec note: v1.0 uses /.well-known/agent-card.json; the older agent.json
path you may see in v0.x examples is out of date.
🔑 Key insight
A2A turns any agent into a network service with a public business card. Discover the
agent through its Agent Card, then pick the execution mode that fits the work:
synchronous for fast replies, asynchronous Tasks for long jobs, streaming for live
progress, and push notifications for unpredictable timing.
Message or Task is always Agent B's choice — so Agent A must handle both.
